title: What Was Mecca Like Before Islam?
description:
Watch Fighting For the Vote here: https://nebula.tv/videos/extrahistory-fighting-for-the-vote-episode-1?ref=religionforbreakfast
With my link, you can get 50% off of Nebula. It’s just $30/year, or $2.5/month, at https://go.nebula.tv/religionforbreakfast 

What was Mecca actually like before Islam? Drawing on the latest historical research, we explore the city's population, trade, pilgrimage traditions, and religious diversity...and challenge some longstanding assumptions about Muhammad's birthplace.

00:00 Mecca: A Historical Black Box
2:28 Hijaz Explained and Lack of Evidence
7:26 A Town not a City
9:12 A Trade Hub?
14:17 A Pilgrimage Hub?
19:05 A Religiously Diverse Town
25:51 Nebula is awesome, seriously, big fan


Religion for Breakfast videos take a lot of research and collaboration. Patreon support helps fund editors, scholars, and future episodes. Support us here: https://www.patreon.com/c/religionforbreakfast

segments.text: The historian FE Peters once wrote that the Quran is as little interested in Mecca as the Gospels are in Nazareth. So think about Nazareth and the Gospels.
They tell us that it's a town in the Galilee where Jesus grows up, but not much beyond that. If you wanted to reconstruct what Nazareth was actually like in the first century, like how big
was it? What was daily life like? The Gospels aren't much help as a historical source because Nazareth is just kind of there. It's mentioned mostly in passing.
We see something similar with Mecca in the Quran. According to the traditional Islamic chronology, Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE. Began preaching
there around 610. But the Quran mentions Mecca by name only once. Only once in the entire book. Now, sure, it
references the sacred house, the Cabba, and some of the rituals associated with it. But it tells us surprisingly little about Mecca as a settlement. So, what would you actually have seen if you
visited Mecca in the year 600, just a decade before Muhammad began preaching?
According to the traditional Muslim accounts, Mecca was already an important religious center. Muhammad's tribe, the Kuresh, controlled the sanctuary at the Cabba and made their living partly
through trade. Later, Muslim historians describe pilgrims visiting the city to worship Arabian gods with some 360 idols
gathered around the Cabba. But most of these descriptions come from Muslims writing long after Muhammad's lifetime.
Ibn Ashak was an Arab historian who composed one of the earliest biographies of Muhammad, but composed around the middle of the 8th century, more than 120
years after Muhammad's death. In fact, excavations in the city's historic center have long been restricted, and the Saudi government's construction
projects in Mecca have destroyed valuable historical remains. And we don't have a single securely identified reference to Mecca in any surviving
pre-Islamic Greek, Latin, Syriak, or Persian sources. When it comes to the historical record, preIslamic Mecca is something of a black box. Pun 100%
intended. As the historian Sulle Mando puts it in his book, Before the Quran, those who dig deeper into the history of this region before Islam are often
surprised to learn that there's not a single non-Muslim source that knows about the existence of Mecca before the emergence of Islam. He goes on to say
that if we set aside later Muslim histories for a moment, the familiar picture of Mecca being a bustling trading town with a temple of idols
receiving visitors from all corners of Arabia is a mirage. So with all this in mind, let's try to answer what was Mecca actually like before Islam. I'm Dr.
Andrew Henry, scholar of religion. This is Religion for Breakfast. Mecca is located in a region called the Hijaz.
It's a mountainous western strip of the Arabian Peninsula inland from the Red Sea. There's a lot of desert and of course a lot of sand. It's coarse and rough and irritating and it gets
everywhere. But if you've seen photographs of Mecca's landscape, you'll notice the immediate surroundings are really dominated by mountains. The settlement occupies a valley hemmed in
by steep rocky hills. It's not the most hospitable place to say the least. In fact, the name Hijaz means barrier,
referring to the mountains separating the coastal plane to the west from the plateau to the east. But the hij also had a long history of settled life.
Especially in the north, towns developed around oases where reliable water supplies allowed people to irrigate crops. These include places like TA and
Kbar. Yathre the settlement later known as Medina also belongs to this world of oases settlements. And some of these urbanized areas were pretty big. At
Kbar, about 600 km north of Mecca, archaeologists have identified a wall built around 2,000 BC that originally stretched for about 14 1.5 km. The walls
of these oases could enclose agricultural fields along with residential areas. So people have been building and maintaining substantial settlements in this part of Arabia for
thousands of years before Islam. We also have ancient written references to some of these places. Yathr for example, later Medina appears in an inscription
left by the south Arabian ruler Abraa in the 550 CE only a few decades before Muhammad's lifetime. And the second century geographer Talamy mentions a
settlement called Lothropa writing around 145 CE. Scholars generally identified this with Yatre, but Mecca is harder to find in our historical
sources. The scholar Steven Shoemaker writes, "It is generally surprising how little we actually know about the social and economic conditions of the Quran's
traditional milyu during the early 7th century. To a certain extent, the severe limitations of our evidence for this region have largely foresstalled any
efforts to critically investigate the history of Mecca and Yathre in late antiquity. Now the geographer Tommy who I just mentioned might give us our
earliest written reference to Mecca. In the same work where he mentions Yathre as Latha he lists another settlement in western Arabia called Macakaraba. Now he
doesn't describe the place or really tell us anything about it. He simply gives us a name and a set of coordinates. Macaraba 73° and 20 minutes
longitude 22° latitude. For centuries scholars identified Macaraba with Mecca.
And if they're right, this would be a reference to Mecca nearly 500 years before Muhammad. The historian Ian Morris writes, "The coordinates put it
roughly in the right place, and the name looks about half right, but emphasis on the half right." In the same study, Morris challenged this identification.
First, Tomy's coordinates are off. He places Macaraba too far inland to the southeast of Yathre where Mecca is
almost directly south of Medina. Now, that's not necessarily a dealbreaker.
Tomy's coordinates for Arabia are often inaccurate, particularly when it comes to longitude. As Morris writes, Tommy apparently had more trouble calculating
longitude than latitude, meaning that his towns are more accurately positioned north south than east west. So, Macaraba could still be somewhere near Mecca.
Morris thinks there's a bigger problem with the name, though. The problem remains that Macaraba and Mecca are different words. If we see Mecca in the
first half of Macakaraba, then we need to explain the second half. If Mecca is an abbreviation of Macakaraba, then we should ideally want to explain how that
came about. And if Macakaraba is an epithet for Mecca, that too demands an explanation. And he argues that there hasn't been a convincing answer. Morris
traces nearly 400 years of people trying to answer how Macaraba could refer to Mecca beyond the argument, well, they sound kind of similar. The
identification goes back to a scholar named Samuel Bokart who in 1646 proposed that Macakaraba came from Makkah Rabba
meaning great Mecca. Later scholars rejected this and proposed other explanations. One influential theory derives Macakaraba from an ancient South
Arabian word meaning temple or sanctuary written with the consonants M krb. That sounds promising given the Cabba. But
why would a settlement in the Hijaz have a South Arabian name? And how would that word have become Mecca? Morris examines these competing explanations and finds
none of them convincing. He also points out that no other ancient source mentions Macaraba and no medieval Muslim geographer ever calls Mecca by that
name. Now, other scholars have continued to defend it. But they've proposed different explanations of the name which Morris also finds unconvincing. But just
because we can't confidently identify Mecca in non-Arabic sources, doesn't mean Mecca didn't exist. As I mentioned, the Quran itself, a valuable ancient
source from the 7th century, mentions Mecca by name. In surah 48:4, it refers to events taking place in the valley of Mecca. Other passages describe the
sacred house and its rituals. We also have Arabic poetry that mentions the Cabba and pilgrims traveling to Mecca.
And as we'll see, the historian Peter Webb makes a compelling case that some of these poems preserve genuine pre-Islamic material. So, there's good reason to think that Mecca was already
an established settlement with a religious sanctuary before Muhammad began preaching. The question [clears throat] remains, though, how significant was it? First, we need to
get this out of the way. We're not talking about a huge city here. It's located in a rather barren part of the Hijaz, nowhere near a major oasis,
meaning it didn't have a lot of water and didn't have enough agricultural land to support a large population. Some estimates placed the pre-Islamic population at only a few hundred people.
In a 2022 article, the historian Majid Robinson calculated that Mecca around Muhammad's lifetime may have had around 550 people. Now, obviously, nobody was
walking around in ancient Mecca conducting a census. And because there haven't been any excavations here, we can't make any population estimates based on an excavated neighborhood.
Robinson arrived at this estimate using a 9th century book called the genealogy of the Curesh, which preserves extensive records of the families belonging to
Muhammad's tribe, like records of the fathers, their sons, brothers, and their marriages. From this genealogy, Robinson identified 131 adult men from Muhammad's
generation. He then used a statistical model to examine their family relationships, particularly how many of them were brothers. The results led him to argue that the genealogy might
preserve something close to a complete record of the adult men of that generation rather than just naming the most famous guys in the settlement.
Estimating from that figure of 131 men to account for women, children, and the enslaved population, Robinson arrived at a total population of 552 people living
in Mecca. Now, it's fair to question whether a genealogy compiled more than 200 years after Muhammad can really give us a reliable population estimate. And
Robinson's calculation involves several assumptions, and we can't be sure how many people these records might have left out. Robinson's broader conclusion,
though, is defensible. That Mecca probably had hundreds of inhabitants rather than thousands. Now, we can't independently verify the estimate, but
if it's even roughly correct, we should probably change our terminology. We're talking about a village here, not a city. The debate comes down to the
nature of this village. Was it a sleepy, out of the way place, or surprisingly wealthy and well-connected given its size and obscurity? For a long time,
historians assumed that Mecca was a wealthy trading center. According to the traditional accounts, merchants from the Curesh made a fortune transporting goods
along caravan routes between southern Arabia and the Roman Empire. This idea became very influential through the work of 20th century scholars. Scholars like Henri Lmens and W. Montgomery Watt.
Watts biographies of Muhammad described Mecca as a prosperous commercial community while Llmens argued that Mecca was a wealthy financial center of a vast international network of spice traders.
And in the Quran, there is some indication that Meccans engaged in trade. Surah 106 briefly mentions the Curesh making customary winter and
summer journeys. Now, the passage doesn't tell us the destinations or tell us what they were transporting, but later interpreters argue that they were embarking on trading expeditions. For
example, the 9th and 10th century scholar Al Tabari in his commentary on Karan 106 preserves reports that the cares traveled to Syria in the summer and Yemen in the winter to trade.
However, scholars in recent decades have argued that this image of Mecca as a major trade hub is vastly overblown. In 1987, the historian Patricia Crona
published Meccan trade and the rise of Islam, which seriously challenged the conventional picture. She examined the trade routes of late antiquity and argued that there's little evidence that
Mecca was an important stopping point in international commerce. The ancient accounts of goods moving between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean don't
mention Mecca as a major center and the settlement was also well inland from the Red Sea, not exactly a port city and was located off several routes that
historians had proposed. Krono was also skeptical of later descriptions of the Curesh being wealthy. There's a story, for instance, that Muhammad's great-grandfather secured permission
from the Byzantine authorities for Meccans to sell their goods in Syria.
Other traditions have Muhammad himself trading animal hides. Historians such as Crona doubt these stories in part because they were composed well after
the events they claim to describe. More recently, the scholar Steven Shoemaker has taken a very skeptical position. In his 2022 book, Creating the Quran, he
describes Mecca as a small settlement whose economy was probably based primarily on raising livestock. He writes, "Mecca was therefore no major
center of international trade, but rather a small remote village with a subsistence economy based in pastoralism." Following Crona, Shoemaker
also questions whether Mecca was conveniently located to serve as a caravan stop and that Mecca Medina were by all indications at the beginning of
the 7th century small, sleepy, out of the way places with little economic or other significance to the outside world.
Now, other scholars have pushed back against this camp. In a 2010 article, the historian Mikuel Bukarin argued that Mecca was indeed connected to the
caravan routes linking South Arabia with the Mediterranean. He points to several pieces of evidence. One is an inscription from an Axomite king describing military efforts to secure
trade routes in Western Arabia. He also argues that based on the geography of Western Arabia that an important caravan route could have passed through Mecca.
He concludes that the incense trade survived in Muhammad's lifetime and that the Meccans were big players in this economy. But much of this evidence comes
from places outside of Mecca and from several centuries before Muhammad.
Shoemaker, for one, is unconvinced, saying that Bkharin's argument is fully unpersuasive since it relies on later
evidence from the Islamic tradition and frequent improbable speculations.
Interestingly, Crona herself didn't rule out all long-distance trade. See, later Islamic sources say that the Curesh traded in leather and animal hides. And
Crona thinks there might be a historical kernel of truth here because of the Roman army. They needed an enormous amount of leather for equipment. Based
on one estimate, a Roman legion of around 5,000 soldiers would require the skins of more than 65,000 goats just to
make their tents. And that's just one legion. So supplying the Roman military could have made you a ton of money.
Though Crona herself acknowledges that this theory is speculative. She can't prove that the cures supplied the Roman military or even that the merchants described in these later accounts were
based in Mecca. Sullean offers a somewhat more moderate perspective, but even he agrees with Shoemaker and Crona that we should not imagine Mecca as a
prosperous commercial center supported by the great incense trade of earlier centuries. He writes that by all indications it was a small settlement.
Where do pushes back is on the idea that Mecca was isolated from the wider world.
He points out that centuries of caravan traffic had helped establish substantial towns in the Hijaz and these towns were connected by routes running between
northern and southern Arabia. The great incense trade had declined long before Muhammad's lifetime. But those routes had not disappeared. Neither had the
cultural and religious connections they helped to create. So even in Do's more moderate reconstruction, we should not picture Mecca as a wealthy trading hub.
It was a small settlement. And the real debate ranges from shoemaker who argues that Mecca was isolated from and insignificant to the broader world of
late antiquity to scholars like dost who say that this is an overstatement. He argues Mecca was located within a region that had a long history of commerce, urbanism and contact with its neighbors.
Now whether or not Mecca was a trade hub though we can say with a bit more certainty that it was a pilgrimage hub at least on a regional scale. Majid
Robinson suggests that the cures developed what he calls a religio mercantile project around the middle of the 500 CE. In his reconstruction, a
relatively small community established relationships with neighboring tribes through a combination of trade and religious activities centered on the
Cabba. Pilgrimage has a long history in Arabian religion. In his 2022 book, The Religion and Rituals of the Nomads of
Pre-Islamic Arabia, the historian Akan Al Jalad examines ancient rock inscriptions written in Safety, a script used by nomadic communities in northern
Arabia to write the various forms of old Arabic. These inscriptions already use a word for pilgrimage, hag, closely
related to the Arabic word Hajj. They also use hag as a verb, meaning to perform a pilgrimage. One inscription even records that its authors set off on
the pilgrimage. Another refers to a year when a pilgrimage to a sanctuary in what's now southern Syria failed to take place. Now, these inscriptions come from
much farther north than Mecca, and they generally date to centuries before Muhammad's lifetime. They don't tell us anything directly about the Cabba, but
they show us that pilgrimage to sacred places was already an established religious practice among Arabian communities long before Islam. And the
Cabba itself appears to have a history stretching back before Muhammad. A Christian chronicle written in Syriak around 660 CE mentions an Arabian sanctuary called the Tent of Abraham.
According to the chronicler, Arabs had been worshiping and offering sacrifices there for generations. Now, the text doesn't explicitly name Mecca, but some
scholars identify the sanctuary with the Cabba, possibly as a tent-like structure before the cube-shaped building was built. So, there's reason to think that
the Cabba was already an established sanctuary site before Islam. And we have some evidence that pilgrims traveled there. The historian Peter Webb addressed this question in a 2023
article called the Hajj before Muhammad where he examined pre-Islamic Arabic poetry that references Mecca's sanctuary and its rituals. Now, there are some
problems with using poetry as a historical source. These poems were collected generations after Muhammad, and some of the verses were probably
invented or altered, but Webb argues that several poems preserve genuine pre-Islamic material. One example comes from Al-Nabiga al- Dubani, a poet who
lived in the late 500s CE. In one of his poems, he swears an oath. I swear by the life of he whose cabba I have circled,
and I swear by the thick blood poured upon the sacrifice stones. The poem goes on to mention birds protected within the sacred precinct and travelers approaching Mecca between two wells.
Now, there's a lot of information packed into these lines that sheds light on Mecca in the late 500s. We have a late sixth century poet mentioning a
sanctuary that people traveled to and a ritual circumambulation of the Cabba which is just the fancy term of walking around it. A central ritual for Islam
today. He also mentions animals being sacrificed on stones called Ansab. All of these are recognizable features of pilgrimage in late antique Arabia. Other
poems give us additional details about pilgrimage to Mecca before Islam. The poet Zuher ibn Abisulma mentions pilgrims camping at a site called Mina
and shaving their hair. Both of which remain part of the Hajj today where Mina is the pilgrimage campground located 6 km southwest of Mecca. I swore solemnly
by the campsites of Mina and by the shaven forlocks and lice laden hair.
Another poet mentions pilgrims gathering beneath Mount H and the blood of sacrificial animals. I swear by him to whose precincts the curesh make
pilgrimage and by the gatherings under Mount Hia and by the holy month of Banu Omaya. Webb argues that these lines probably preserve an authentic
pre-Islamic reference to the Curesh tribe and their relationship with the Cabba. And there's reason to think that the Curesh had a role in the sanctuary
before Muhammad began preaching, even if we can't establish exactly how their authority was organized. So from these poems, we can begin to imagine what
someone visiting Mecca around 600 CE might have encountered. Pilgrims travel to the Cabba bringing animals for sacrifice and gathering at sacred sites
in the surrounding landscape like at Mina. The real question is if we can call Mecca a major pilgrimage hub at this time. According to later Islamic
accounts, people travel to the Cabba from all across Arabia. But Webb finds a more limited picture in the poetry. Most of the references to the Meccan
pilgrimage come from poets who already lived in the Haj. He says there's a virtual absence of illusions to Mecca amongst poets from outside of the Hijaz.
So he argues that the preIslamic Hajj was primarily a regional pilgrimage.
People from further away might have made a pilgrimage to Mecca, but we don't have evidence for the enormous panabian gathering described in later Islamic
accounts. The scholar Ilka Lindstead also argues that the Cabba was not the only and probably not the most important shrine or pilgrimage destination in the
Arabian Peninsula, but it was of local importance. So, who were the people of Mecca in the year 600? According to
later Muslim historians, Mecca was predominantly a polytheistic community before Islam. One hadith describes Muhammad finding 360 idols around the Cabba when he conquered it in 630 CE.
And according to the 9th century historian Iban Al Kalbi, idol worship was part of everyday life. He claims that every family in Mecca kept an idol
at home and before setting out on a journey, someone would touch the idol, hoping for a safe trip. when they returned, they would touch it again in gratitude. Though historians in recent
years have questioned these accounts, returning to that pre-Islamic pilgrimage poetry we're just talking about, Peter Webb noticed that poets generally invoke
a single deity at the Cabba, apparently Allah. They don't describe a sanctuary filled with different gods. One poet
does mention the gods Allat and Aluza being worshiped at Mecca. The Quran itself does mention three Arabian deities by name, Allot, Aluza, and
Manat. But it also suggests that Muhammad's opponents already recognized Allah as the creator of the universe. In surah 39:3, the Quran describes people
explaining why they worship other beings. We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah. Recent discoveries have prompted scholars to
argue that these so-called polytheists of Mecca might have been more monotheistic in their orientation than was previously assumed. In a 2026
article, Ahmed Al Jalad and Heitham Sidki examined a collection of pre-Islamic Arabic inscriptions from Western Arabia. Earlier incriptions invoke different Arabian gods, including
the goddess All. But in the surviving 6th century inscriptions, the only god invoked is Allah or Alah, which means
God. One pre-Islamic inscription discovered only 90 km from Mecca mentions a man identifying himself as Abuza, a name meaning servant of Al-
Usuza, a pagan name. But the inscription invokes God and urges people to be righteous toward Allah. Scholars such as Al Jalad and Lindstead argue that we can
catch a glimpse here of the religious environment of Mecca in late antiquity.
What we could call pagan monotheism or henotheism, the belief in multiple gods, but the elevation and worship of one god
in particular. Scholars like Algelad and Sidki proposed that Arabian religion had been undergoing a monotheizing transformation in the centuries before
Islam. Allah was already known as a creator god in older Arabian religion, but he was increasingly identified with the supreme god of Jewish and Christian
traditions. Meanwhile, some of the older Arabian gods had been demoted, reinterpreted as lesser supernatural
beings or intercessors. Now, this is a scholarly reconstruction and most of these inscriptions were not discovered in Mecca itself. But the evidence
suggests that Muhammad's religious environment was already being shaped by centuries of contact with monotheistic traditions. Lindstead writes, "The West
Arabia material record indicates that people had come to embrace monotheist beliefs already by the time the prophet Muhammad was born and indeed in some
cases centuries before that. In fact, Lindstead argues that there were probably Christians and Jews in pre-Islamic Mecca." In a recent study titled, "The religious groups of Mecca
and Medina in the sixth and seventh centuries," he suggests that we've underestimated the religious diversity of these settlements and that later Islamic tradition downplayed the
presence of Christians and Jews and exaggerated the presence of polytheists.
One detail comes from the 9th century Meccan historian Alzraki, who mentions a place called the cemetery of the Christians. He doesn't tell us where the
cemetery was established, so we can't confidently date it to Muhammad's lifetime. But it's an interesting clue that there was probably multiple generations of Christians living in
Mecca. And the 9th century historian Alakubi claims that entire branch of the cares had converted to Christianity. A pre-Islamic Christian Arab poet named
Adi Iban Zade reportedly swore an oath by the Lord of Mecca and of the cross.
If the verse is authentic, it suggests that at least some Christians in the region thought their god was linked with the Meccan sanctuary. Now the evidence
for Judaism in Mecca is thinner. The historians Michael Leer and Esan Ruhi have identified later accounts describing men from the Kuresh who married Jewish women or had Jewish
mothers. Lindstead also points to several passages in the Quran itself, usually linked with Muhammad's mechan preaching that refer to people familiar with Jewish and Christian scripture. In
surah 10:94, Muhammad is even told to consult people who have been reading earlier revelations. And surah 28:52-55
describes how some people among the people of the book accepted the revelations received by Muhammad.
Lindstead interprets this as evidence that Jews and Christians were part of Muhammad's immediate religious environment. The scholar Gabriel say Reynolds makes a similar case in his
2025 book Christianity and the Quran. He draws on Al Jalad and Sidki's work on monotheistic inscriptions near Mecca and adds evidence from the Quran itself like
the story from the Quran called the companions of the cave. According to the story, a group of young men miraculously slept for centuries. A very similar
story circulated earlier among Christians, and the Quran even addresses disagreements about how many sleepers there were and how long they slept.
Reynolds argues that this suggests the Quran's original audience included people already familiar with this story and invested in debates about it, which
for him indicates Christian communities must have formed a substantial presence in the religious environment where the Quran emerged. Now, not everyone agrees
with how much we can conclude from this evidence. The scholar Nikolai Sinai, for example, suggests that knowledge of Christianity could have reached Mecca through travelers and preachers without
requiring a substantial resident Christian community. And because there haven't been any thoroughgoing excavations in Mecca, we simply don't
have the archaeological evidence to tell us whether there were churches, synagogues, or organized Jewish and Christian communities in Mecca around the year 600. But it's very likely that
Mecca in the year 600 was a religiously diverse settlement with Jews, Christians, and possibly monotheists who didn't belong to either tradition as
well. So, what was PreIslamic Mecca actually like? Based on the available evidence, PreIslamic Mecca was probably a relatively small settlement in an

agriculturally poor valley of Western Arabia. The people living there depended on relationships with neighboring communities for essential supplies. But we should not exaggerate that it was some kind of international trading hub.
Though, even though Mecca was a very small town, it was probably religiously diverse. As Lindstead writes, apparently the Cabba shrine there served as a
regional pilgrimage site that drew people from different faith communities.
But despite its humble beginnings, over the following centuries, Mecca became one of the most important religious places in the entire world. And as its
importance grew, Muslim historians began telling increasingly elaborate stories about its pre-Islamic past. The Quran links the Cabba with Abraham and
Ishmamail. But by the 9th and 10th centuries, Muslim historians were tracing the sanctuary's history all the way back to Adam. According to these accounts, after being expelled from
paradise, Adam traveled to Mecca and performed the first pilgrimage. Noah's ark floated around the Cabba seven times during the flood. There are even later
Islamic accounts of Alexander the Great making the pilgrimage. Mecca's importance in the Islamic world encouraged writers to place it at the
center of a much earlier history. As a historian, I see this sort of thing all the time. Just because something seems historically important to us today
doesn't mean people at the time recognized its significance. That's something explored in a new series from my fellow creators at Extra History.
It's called Fighting for the Vote. It's an amazing animated series examining the history of women's suffrage in the US and beyond. With their signature

a movement we often remember as a unified struggle for political equality was actually shaped by competing factions and serious disagreements over
